title: Boreal seed-eater reports at eastern North American feeders followed the two-summer temperature cue of seed crops in 1989-2024, but the cue did not explain their long-term decrease
abstract: Question: do winter reports of irruptive boreal seed-eaters at North American feeders follow the two-summer temperature cue of boreal seed crops (Delta-T = June-July temperature of the summer before the crop minus that of the summer two years before), and can a climate-driven seed-crop change explain their long-term decrease? Earlier campaign work found that losses of these species drove much of the warm-ward change of winter feeder communities but did not test seed crops. Data: 4.0 million Project FeederWatch checklists at 86,957 sites (seasons 1989-2024), CRU TS 4.09 and Berkeley Earth temperature, 37 USGS white spruce cone series (1983-2017) and BBS trends. The plan was written before outcome models. Results: cone crops increased by 0.38 SD per 1 C of local Delta-T. South of 45 N in the east, all five primary taxa (redpolls, Pine Siskin, Evening Grosbeak, Purple Finch, Red-breasted Nuthatch) had fewer reports after a high Delta-T: pooled -0.072 relative-index units per SD (95% CI -0.119 to -0.026) with the boreal box and -0.133 (-0.179 to -0.086) with the eastern boreal box; six non-irruptive controls had +0.001 (-0.004 to +0.006). A Quebec cone index gave the same sign for all five taxa. Planned out-of-sample tests without trend terms gave no forecast gain; post-hoc tests with trends gave 12-23% gains for four taxa. The cue did not explain the long-term decrease: redpoll reports fell 6.1% and Evening Grosbeak reports 11.6% per year south of 45 N, but the Delta-T model implies small increases, free two-summer models imply trends near zero, and the cone series had no trend. Limitations: feeder reports mix abundance and feeder use; large temperature boxes; 36 seasons; cone data mainly from Alaska and Yukon and end in 2017; post-hoc tests are exploratory.

White spruce cone and seed crops (within-series z-scores, 37 series, 1983-2017) against local Delta-T and against the previous summer temperature alone (centred within series). Black points are bin means with 95% intervals.

Left: 1989-2024 trends of FeederWatch reporting indices in three zones and BBS 1966-2025 breeding trends. Right: observed trends south of 45 N and trends implied by the previous-summer model (upper bound, no trend term) and the Delta-T model.

citations.reason: Reported that irruptive finch losses, not winter temperature, drove the winter feeder CTI change; we test the untested seed-crop cause.
Reported species contributions of irruptive finches to the winter CTI trend; we show these trends are not a seed-crop climate effect.
Confirmed the Delta-T cue for Swiss beech pollen; we confirm it for North American white spruce cones and bird irruptions.
